title: Preview: This is not the nostalgia Warriors wanted
text:
Preview: This is not the nostalgia Warriors wanted 
 Subscribe Sign in Preview: This is not the nostalgia Warriors wanted
 Breakdowns everywhere!
 punk basketball Nov 18, 2026 16 44 Share There’s a lot breaking down all over the world, but especially here in the United States right now. The Golden State Warriors are not immune. Neither is the pozole at my office. It used to be soooo good. I don’t know what happened there. For the Warriors, the root cause is easy to diagnose. 
 Already hamstrung by injuries with long-term recovery windows, the Warriors are up to nearly 70% of their total roster payroll sitting on the injury list now that Steph Curry has joined those ranks. With Al Horford (back) and Draymond Green (elbow) both listed as Questionable tonight against the Dallas Mavericks, that number could climb much higher. 1 
 This could hearken back to one of the weirdest Warriors games I’ve ever witnessed in my life. Actually, there’s two, but one way or another, this is going to be a historic night that might just end up in a win, against all odds. 
 The Dallas Mavericks sit right below Golden State in the standings, having dropped three straight on their own way deeper into trouble. Unlike the Warriors, the Mavs have their main players on the court, but Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving haven’t been enough. 
 GAME DETAILS 
 WHO: Golden State Warriors (8-6) at Dallas Mavericks (7-7) 
 WHEN: Tuesday, November 18th, 2026; 5pm PDT 
 WATCH: ESPN (maybe NBCSBA??), YouTubeTV 
 Injuries: 
 Systems fail 
 There’s a lot of uncertainty in the NBA, so team managers go through a lot of scenarios, trying to figure out which way to lean if something bad happens. These contingency plans are gambles at best - can Bassey cover a starting position if needed, for example - but there are well-educated guesses behind the intersection of impacts and likelihoods. 
 The loss of Curry has proven to be every bit as catastrophic as feared. The entire system is built around his presence. That presence is still as impactful as ever, but it’s more fragile now. After all those miles bumping and running across the NBA hardwood, Curry’s body is beginning to have to pay the debt for all that gravity he’s created. 
 There’s a really poignant article about Curry in ESPN that is worth your time, but if nothing else, all of Dub Nation needs to hear this so we can all anguish together. 
 “Against Detroit, it took everything in me down there on the training table just to be like, ‘Oh, I can go out here tonight and play,’” Curry said. “And I was just faking it for the first whatever [25 minutes].”
 There’s something poetic about his final sequence before he left the game. Curry came off a third-quarter pindown into an isolation against Ausar Thompson and did what he described as “a high-step thing because it hurt so bad in that moment.”
 After the fidget, Curry shook Thompson with a crossover combination, hobbled into the lane and poured in an and-1 floater over one of the best perimeter defenders in the world to give him 23 points in those 25 minutes.
 But then he limped to the sideline and told Rick Celebrini -- the franchise’s lead medical decision-maker whom Curry trusts implicitly -- that the swelling and stiffness had become too much to bear. 
 Now, I won’t get into the nature of collective consciousness in grief, but given the deep crap storm that is flowing right now, a bit of historical perspective might help us all. 
 Look, the Warriors got smoked by the lowly New Orleans Pelicans. Yes it was a revenge game, but before we single out the team’s poor shooting from deep as the cause - 11 of 46 as a team in their last game (23.9%) - it’s valuable to understand just how far down the list of plans this roster has come. But it’s honestly okay because it’s a glimpse of the future, for better or worse. 
 I don’t know how historically bad this current viable roster is, but assuming Green and Horford don’t play this game could get comical. For us old heads, this hearkens back to yore in a way that’s sure to bring out a bemused chuckle. 
 Let me take us back. November 24th, 2009. 
 Coach Don Nelson had six players available. Well, scratch that: Nellie was out, and assistant coach Keith Smart was calling the shots. But the six-player part is right, and one of them was rookie Stephen Curry. The beginning of his NBA journey!
 Mikki Moore and Anthony Randolph (the lone bench player) both played just over 30 minutes, while Curry logged nearly 35. Monta Ellis, Anthony Morrow and Vladimir Radmanović never left the floor, playing all 48 minutes in a 111-103 win over Dallas. Overall, the six players who appeared accounted for every minute of the game, combining for just $23.3 million in annual salaries.
 In the words of interim coach, Keith Smart, there was nothing to prove any more.
 “Coming into this game, we had nothing to lose,” said assistant coach Keith Smart, who filled in for Nelson . “The worst case is they blow us out and we move on to [Wednesday night’s game in San Antonio]. But our guys have a lot of character. They played hard together and made the right decisions.” 
 It’s hard to remember other times where the roster was as depleted as it is now. With so many key starters on long-term injured reserve… I don’t want to pick too hard at those memories, and yet I do. 
 I had to dig, but there was an even rougher game, weirdly enough the very next year, same season. On April 14th, 2010, there was an even weirder game, and again the Warriors won. In this instance, The Warriors technically played eight players, but Anthony Morrow and Ronny Turiaf had to clock into the game just to keep the team from a forfeit after Devean George picked up six fouls - after both Chris Hunter and then Anthony Tolliver got hurt. Again, rookie Curry played every single minute, this time scoring what was then a career-high 42 points.
 Why do I bring this up now?
 Because the Warriors are pretty close to that historic level of roster drought. I’m going to leave it up to the rest of the internet to tell me whether or not tonight’s team is the lowest percent of available team salary ever, but it’s got to be close. 
 So sure, let’s watch Yax’s efficiency, and hope that the Warriors’ team defense can handle their assignments tonight. But keep the broader perspective in your heart. The plan isn’t all that complicated, but collapsing on Kyrie Irving and Cooper Flagg and being able to recover is a legitimate test of a team’s defense. These are the sorts of challenges that even bad teams have to learn how to meet. 
 This era of Warriors basketball is all about the closing stanza of the Curry opera. Part of that oratory has got to entail a few slaps in the face. This is what post-Curry basketball feels like - a whole lot like pre-Curry basketball, weirdly enough. 
 Look at the rebuilding sagas of the Brooklyn Nets, or the Utah Jazz. There’s no promises that what comes after this will be better. Kind of like the internet and AI. You can expect some cool stuff, but the slow trajectory is one of decay, not improvement. 
 Those cautionary tales aside, this next month (or so) will give players like Yax and Podz some useful perspective. There’s not always going to be some superstar that will come and save you. The team has to be good enough to win, as-is. The players themselves are going to have to learn how to be more impactful. 
 I can’t help but point out that the lone standing vet, and highest-paid available player has been fine, but Green has been far from dominant in this stretch - which again, points the youth movement towards the direction they’ll need to go from here in order to succeed. He’s not a detriment, but it’s simply not enough lift without Curry. 
 Draymond Green in the absence of Curry This isn’t about the old system any more. Wiseman is gone. Anthony Randolph won some rings overseas. Neither one of those things matters right now. 
 Until the old system comes back online, the rest of this roster is going to have to figure it out for themselves. I don’t think the lesson learned in San Antonio was that this team sucks, it was more that they’ve got to do better. The new core - Yax, Podz, Melton - have been solid, but just short of enough. Well, to be fair, at times it’s felt like a much larger gap than that. 
 Now, tonight’s opponent has flaws of their own. The Mavs have one of the worst three-point percentages in the league (33.5%, ranked 24th in the NBA), but that’s far from their only problem. Much like the Warriors, this Mavericks team has been wracked with injuries and continuity issues. 
 It’s funny because so much of the Warriors recent failures stem from poor shooting. It’s hard to not oversimplify game - after all, easier shots go in. 
 The Warriors have had a crutch for far too long. 2 
 There’s a difference between looking good in a functioning Warriors lineup and being able to keep a Warriors lineup functioning. Curry has made a lot of people look better for a very long time. His gravity creates advantages before anyone else touches the ball; his presence changes the geometry of the floor, the quality of a teammate’s shot, and the amount of defensive attention everyone else has to absorb. That’s an extraordinary environment in which to develop. It can also obscure some deficiencies. Without him, the margins disappear. The reads have to be quicker, the decisions cleaner, and the individual matchups suddenly matter a whole lot more. That’s the test now. 
 Yax and Podz have earned some leeway with the coaches, Bassey and Melton have shown some incredibly interesting flashes. But now everything is stripped away. It’s not “six available” players like Curry’s rookie season, but the wheel of time has turned all the way over now and there’s a new generation that will either sink or swim. 
 This is all temporary, like Keith Smart. 
 In a month, it will be the middle of December, and maybe Curry is back; but more importantly, that timeline presumably includes updates on Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody too. Everything inching closer to the actual plan. 
 Tonight’s game plan is much closer to a general directive. Fight. Survive. The lessons learned better not be that this team sucks without Curry. 
 Prediction 
 Not being able to win without 85% of your total salary available isn’t something to be ashamed of, nonetheless, I’d like to see the remaining 15% shock the world tonight. The underdog Warriors have beaten the Mavs before, they’ll do it again tonight, but it’ll be a close one. 
 1 Ugh fine, I did the math. It’s not a whole lot higher. Adding in Green and Horford would be 85.3% of the Warriors salary out tonight. 
 2 Or not long enough, am I right? Gimme more Stephen Curry crutch! I’ll take a 76 year-old playing that Kyle Korver role where he slow drifts away from help defenses, even though you know that he’s only got one weapon in him, he’s still knocking down threes all over the place. I’m 90 at that point, high fiving like a young man, despite the arthritis.
